Good morning, Senator Baldacci, Rep Salisbury, and members of the Committee. I am Representative Bill Pluecker, representing House District 44, made up of Warren, Hope, and Union. I appreciate the opportunity to present to you LD 2158, "An Act to Address Vacancies on the Knox County Budget Committee."
Knox County's Budget Committee, requiring five members for a quorum, currently has only four seated members. The remaining five seats stand vacant following the November 2024 election, which produced no candidates from odd-numbered districts. Without a quorum, the Committee cannot legally convene--and critically, cannot fill its own vacancies. We are trapped in a legal deadlock our Charter never anticipated.
This isn't merely procedural. Knox County cannot adopt a 2026 budget, amend the current budget, or plan for 2027. We face indefinite interim budget operations, threatening essential services including public safety for our 18 municipalities. These municipalities depend on timely tax assessments to prepare their own budgets--we risk cascading fiscal instability across our entire county.
Four qualified residents, nominated by their municipal officers, are ready to serve. However, our Commissioners lack authority to appoint them. LD 2159 provides that temporary authority while respecting local input through municipal nominations.
This bill is carefully crafted. It expires April 1, 2029, giving Knox County time to amend our Charter while protecting against a recurrence in the 2028 election cycle. The emergency preamble is essential--our municipalities need immediate clarity for budget planning.

District 44: Hope, Union, & Warren

The Office of the Maine Attorney General confirms our legal predicament. LD 2158 offers the only viable path forward, restoring representative democracy and fiscal stability. Without it, Knox County cannot fulfill its fundamental obligation to its citizens.
I urge this Committee's support for LD 2159. Thank you.

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government:
My name is Marjorie E. Stratton, and I am the Town Manager representing the Town of Vinalhaven. I am writing to you today to urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 2158, An Act to Address Vacancies on the Knox County Budget Committee.
I am submitting this testimony not just as a resident, but as one of the few town members who cannot complete their budget due to the paralysis of government.
The Knox County Budget Committee is supposed to have nine members. Currently, they only have four. Under the Knox County Charter, they need a quorum of five members to conduct any official business. This includes the business of appointing new members to fill vacancies. This bill acts as the "key" to unlock that door, allowing the County Commissioners to temporarily appoint members so they can get back to work.
The towns of Knox County rely on this committee to provide fiscal oversight and ensure tax dollars are spent efficiently. Currently, because of the lack of a quorum to meet or fill vacancies, our towns have effectively lost their seat at the table. This situation leaves municipal taxpayers without their Charter-mandated check on county spending.
Municipal officials need a predictable, transparent county assessment to set their own town budgets and mill rates. The current paralysis creates unnecessary uncertainty for every town in the county. If the Budget Committee cannot function, the budget process stalls, complicating financial planning for our local governments.
LD 2158 is the only viable path to restore this representation. By allowing the vacancies to be filled, you are ensuring that the towns of Knox County once again have a functioning body to protect their financial interests.
I respectfully urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 2158.
Regards,
Marjorie E. Stratton, Town Manager Vinalhaven, Maine (207) 863-2042

Re: Comments of MCCA re LD 2158, An Act to Address Vacancies on the Knox County Budget Committee (Emergency)
Chair Baldacci, Chair Salisbury, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government:
On behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association (MCCA), we appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony in support of LD 2158. MCCA supports this bill as a narrowly tailored, time-sensitive procedural measure that is necessary to allow Knox County to carry out its core budgeting responsibilities while preserving the longer-term role of the county charter and the voters.
About MCCA. Briefly, the Maine County Commissioners Association was established in 1890 to assist Maine's county government in providing vital services to Maine citizens in a responsive, efficient, and credible manner. The Association is based in Augusta, represents all 16 of Maine's counties, and is governed by a board with representation from each participating county.
What does LD 2158 do? Current general law in Maine establishes the Knox County Budget Committee as a nine-member body elected in even-numbered years. Under the Knox County Charter, the Budget Committee may not conduct business without a quorum of at least five members. These two requirements work fine when the Committee has a quorum; however, due to vacancies on the Budget Committee and the failure to fill those vacancies at the 2024 election, the Committee no longer has a quorum and is now unable to perform its statutory duties - approving the Knox County budget. LD 2158 addresses this problem in the short term by providing a temporary alternative method for appointing members to the Budget Committee so that it may regain a quorum and complete its work on the Knox County budget for 2026. The bill would then sunset in 2029.
Why this legislation is necessary. County budgets are foundational to the delivery of essential public services, including public safety, corrections, courts, and administrative functions. Without a functioning budget committee, Knox County cannot move forward with its budget process, creating significant uncertainty and risk. This bill addresses an immediate procedural impasse, not by permanently altering the county's governance structure, but rather by providing a short-term solution that allows the county to function while longer-term options are considered.

Testimony of MCCA re LD 2158 January 28, 2026 Page 2
Charters require time to amend. MCCA strongly supports the role of county charters and local voter control. At the same time, charter amendments are, by design, deliberate processes that require time, public engagement, and ultimately voter approval at a county-wide election. LD 2158 appropriately recognizes that reality. It allows Knox County to meet its immediate budgeting obligations while providing the necessary time and space for the county and its residents to consider whether charter changes are warranted in the future.
Urgency and limited scope. As reflected in the emergency preamble, this legislation must take effect as soon as possible to allow the Budget Committee to complete its work on the 2026 county budget. MCCA views LD 2158 as a practical, narrowly focused response to an unanticipated governance problem, crafted to address the present circumstances without setting broader precedent or undermining the charter process.
Conclusion. For these reasons, the Maine County Commissioners Association supports LD 2158 and respectfully urges the Committee to vote unanimously ought to pass with the emergency preamble. This bill provides Knox County with the tools it needs to fulfill its budgeting responsibilities while preserving the integrity of county charters and local decision-making.
Respectfully submitted,

Commissioner Kevin Kelley, Waldo County

Testimony by Knox County Commissioner Morgan Hynd in Support of LD 2158: An Act to Address Vacancies on the Knox County Budget Committee
Committee on State and Local Government January 28, 2026
Good afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and distinguished members of the
Committee on State and Local Government. My name is Morgan Hynd and I am one of three Knox
County Commissioners. l represent the towns of Washington, Union, Warren, Cushing, Friendship, and
Appleton. l am here to speak in support of LD 2158.
l'd like to start by explaining how Knox County came to require this emergency legislation. As we
approached the beginning of Knox County's budget process in October of 2025, the County's
administrative staff realized that we would be unable to convene the Budget Committee due to the lack of a quorum. Our County Charter requires us to have a quorum to approve new members for the Budget Committee. Because no, one had run in the general election for any of the open seats, we only had four
active members, one short of a quorum. Despite all of the towns providing nominations to fill those empty
seats by October, we had no legal way to approve those nominations.
After seeking the counsel of the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, and our own legal counsel, we determined that the only legal path forward was through emergency legislation that would allow the
County Commissioners to approve one of the five open seats, thereby giving the Budget Committee the quorum needed to approve the remaining four seats.
LD 2158 will sunset on April 1, 2029 which gives Knox County time to review and possibly amend its charter to avoid this situation in the future. This date also carries us through the 2028 election cycle, should we find ourselves in the same position again. That said, county administration and all of our municipalities are now keenly aware of the need to avoid this situation in the future and will do all we can
to fill the seats through the election process moving forward.
Knox County is currently operating under our 2025 budget. This is significantly hampering the County's
ability to function at full capacity, and the consequences will become more acute if we are not able to pass
a 2026 budget. We are fortunate to have great leadership within the County, including our Finance
Director who has worked closely with all departments to maintain critical functions, but we will likely have
to consider more drastic cuts without the support of the Legislature. Our Sheriff is here today to tell you
what that could mean for public safety. We have several other departments that will be impacted as well,
including the Register of Deeds, Probate, the District Attorney's office, the Knox County Regional Airport, and more.
The passage of this emergency legislation is critical to the functioning of Knox County for the remainder of 2026 and for several years ahead. If passed, Knox County will immediately proceed with our budget
process, which will bring relief to our loyal staff, some of whom have worked at the County for decades. It
will also bring stability to our 18 municipal partners, and most importantly to the taxpayers. I respectfully ask that you approve LD 2158 in support of functional government at the county level.

10058808:
Sarah Ann Smith Hope, Maine LD 2158
Regarding LD 2158:
My name is Sarah Ann Smith. I am a citizen of Hope and have been on the Select Board for nine years: during that time I was Vice Chair (2 years I think) and am currently Chair (about four + years), so I am familiar with town and county government, in addition to my experience as a Legislative Assistant to a Congressman and 14 years as a US Foreign Service Officer (diplomat) . I write today in my citizen role and am not speaking for the Select Board or Town of Hope Since I am from away, I have been astounded at what passes for "County Government" in rural Maine compared to the robust county government structures in other states.
As far as I have been able to determine, the only functions Knox County performs are: �Emergency Dispatch Center �Emergency Preparedness �Sheriff's Department (which provides the only police for most of the small towns) �County Jail (currently effectively not functioning)
At the moment, our dispatch is via Waldo County and our prisoners are at Two Bridges in Lincoln County because of the multiple-year crisis in county government.
The current disaster that is Knox County government is a symptom of a state-wide crisis and problem for rural counties where competent leadership, meaning both the Administrator and the elected county commissioners, is scarce. There are simply not enough capable, educated-in-county-government people to run for and hold positions that are part-time and poorly paid (the commissioners) or be fairly compensated for a full-time position (a trained-for-the-job county administrator). Further, there is no oversight whatsoever of what the county does by either the member towns or the citizens. The three elected commissioners can decide what they want, and no matter how much towns and citizens protest their decisions, they do it anyway. In turn, this adversely affects every taxpayer.
That problem will not be solved in the short run. For now, however, it is essential that the entirety of Knox County have continued 911 emergency services and a sheriff's department. Without approval of this emergency bill, that is what will happen because the County cannot muster a quorum because of staffing shortages and people who have left the sinking ship.
In the longer run, the state needs to review the entire structure of government in Maine. It's possible the large counties in southern Maine function well, but in rural Maine, it's a hot mess. Knox has been unable to recruit and retain competent employees and elected commissioners for years, which is what has landed us in this pickle. I expect that other counties are facing similar problems including the ever-escalating costs with no ability for the member towns to have any oversight or control if the county government is failing.
The school system is likewise flawed and requires a state-wide re-set. Unless a town has substantial business or tourist tax income, the entire burden of the ever-escalating costs falls on property owners. In Hope, 79-80 percent of the town budget is for the elementary school and our share of the regional high school. The roads and plowing budget take up a huge amount of the remaining 20 percent. In the 15 years I have lived in Hope, our property taxes have doubled, but our income has most definitely not. The current system causes undue burden on rural property owners, unlike cities and big towns (in the south plus Bangor area).
These systemic flaws are exacerbated by the smaller pool of people in rural Maine who can run for office and fill the jobs with the needed experience. These issues are what have led to the need for today's bill.
Today, I encourage you to pass this bill and allow Knox County to limp along.

Tomorrow, I ask that you begin to address statewide systemic problems in the structure of government, how emergency services are handled (need for regionalization, coordination, less duplication of functions by underfunded towns), and how schools are funded so that the escalating costs do not drive people out of their homes, towns and our wonderful state.
Thank you.
Sarah Ann Smith, Hope, Maine
